abstract: Climate change is already causing widespread losses and damages, and these impacts will intensify as human and natural systems exceed their capacity to adapt. Recent research allows us to understand if and how countries are prioritizing this issue in national policies.

title: Topographic variation shapes organismal responses across mountain landscapes
abstract: Topography is expected to mediate species’ responses to climate change by providing terrain-driven microclimates that buffer animals from warming, yet how topographic shading drives animal responses to climate change remains poorly understood. Using bioenergetic simulations that incorporate topographic shading to predict the ecological and physiological consequences of climate warming, we show that topographic variation can reduce energy expenditure by as much as 20.8% and increase the buffering benefits of shifting elevation by 82.1% for diurnal ectotherms. In contrast, topographic shading provided little buffering for nocturnal ectotherms. Warming also increased energetic costs most at low elevations, widening elevational differences in energetic costs. Across North America, 48.9% of mountain ranges are depleted in topographic features that buffer the effects of warming, with tectonic history shaping present-day terrain-driven microclimates. Together, our results highlight topographic variation as a critical variable shaping organismal experiences of climate change at both landscape and continental scales.

title: Selecting climate solutions creates new institutional authority
Enhancing fairness in climate action through policy packages
abstract: Achieving a fair transition to climate neutrality requires a careful balancing of policy options. Here we quantitatively evaluate the equity implications of different European Union climate policy packages, considering pricing, regulation via standards, subsidies and transfers. Leveraging an integrated modelling framework, we show that standards limit impact variability within income groups, whereas carbon pricing with transfer-based revenue recycling offsets regressive impacts between income groups. Restricting climate policy implementation to either option, therefore, gives rise to a trade-off between horizontal and vertical equity. We then demonstrate numerically how a multi-instrument budget-neutral policy package can resolve this trade-off. Adopting a broader equity perspective that encompasses both horizontal and vertical equity shifts the preferred policy mix towards a combination of standards, pricing, subsidies and transfers. These results provide an explicit, quantified, equity-based rationale for the adoption and acceptability of comprehensive climate policy packages, offering a more nuanced view on policy design.

title: Citizens’ assemblies propose ambitious climate policy but impacts remain limited
abstract: Climate citizens’ assemblies convene randomly selected citizens who, after structured learning and deliberation, develop policy recommendations. Yet, whether they produce more ambitious recommendations and influence political decisions remains contested. Here we conduct a comparative, counterfactual assessment of 488 recommendations from five national and one state-level assembly in Western Europe, drawing on document analysis and expert interviews. The results show that citizens consistently proposed more ambitious climate measures than existing government policy. Recommendations sometimes influenced policy by adding momentum, enriching plans, breaking deadlocks or introducing novel ideas, but such influence was rare. Only the French assembly shows substantial policy impact, with one-third of its recommendations having influenced policy, due to strong power delegation, political leadership and resulting public pressure. In the other cases, policy impact was minimal or absent. These findings show that citizens’ assemblies can raise policy ambition, but translating recommendations into political decisions depends strongly on political conditions.

title: Species hybridization belongs on the climate change agenda
The ambitions and limitations of climate assemblies
abstract: Climate citizens’ assemblies are gaining traction worldwide as a way to involve the public in climate governance. Now a study demonstrates that although these assemblies propose more ambitious recommendations than existing climate policy, these recommendations vary across contexts and have limited impact on policy decisions.

title: Strengthening Rio Convention implementation architecture through reciprocal learning
abstract: As the Rio Conventions mature from negotiating commitments towards delivering them, strengthening implementation has become an urgent priority. We argue for greater cross-convention learning within the context of institutional architecture to accelerate progress on climate, biodiversity and land degradation.

title: Prioritizing demand-side use of clean hydrogen for cost-effective mitigation
abstract: Clean hydrogen can play a pivotal role in decarbonizing ‘hard-to-abate’ sectors. However, it cannot be universally adopted given energy-intensive production, high costs and limited near-term supply. It is therefore critical to prioritize clean hydrogen demands that deliver the most cost-effective emission reductions. Here we evaluate the decarbonization potential and economic costs of clean hydrogen in ten carbon-intensive sectors around 2035. Steelmaking, oil refining and ammonia production emerge as ‘no-regret’ sectors, offering the lowest levelized carbon mitigation costs, whereas hydrogen use in on-road and rail transport is economically unfavourable compared with direct electrification. Although policy support is needed to make clean hydrogen cost-competitive, production incentives are not an effective policy lever for prioritizing its use in ‘no-regret’ sectors. Uniform supply-side subsidies risk misallocating limited clean hydrogen supply and public funds. We conclude that sector-specific demand-side policies are required to align priorities and fully realize the decarbonization potential of clean hydrogen.

title: High wind speed reduces water use efficiency across terrestrial ecosystems
abstract: Wind is a fundamental driver of land–atmosphere exchange, yet its role in ecosystem water use efficiency (WUE) remains unclear. Here using global eddy-covariance observations combined with Earth system model simulations, we show that WUE declines with increasing wind speed across most terrestrial ecosystems, driven primarily by wind-induced increases in evapotranspiration and secondarily by reductions in gross primary productivity. Mechanistically, stronger winds enhance aerodynamic conductance, strengthen ecosystem–atmosphere coupling and amplify atmospheric water demand. Earth system model simulations capture the negative sensitivity of WUE to wind speed and indicate that future WUE changes will be strongly influenced by wind speed. Under high-emission scenarios, intensified reductions in wind speed enhance WUE, whereas weaker stilling under low-emission scenarios reduces this effect. These results establish wind speed as a previously underappreciated regulator of carbon–water coupling and highlight its importance for predicting ecosystem responses to climate change.

title: Combining climate policy instruments for a just transition to a climate-neutral economy
abstract: A distributional analysis of European Union climate policy pathways traces the costs of reducing carbon dioxide emissions to the level of households based on their spending and income patterns. We find that different equity considerations, including income inequality and within-group impact divergence, can shape optimal climate policy design with carbon prices, transfers, standards and subsidies.

title: Warming-driven lower-tropospheric stratification intensifies ducting over global oceans
abstract: Under global warming, the marine atmospheric boundary layer shows an increase in lower-tropospheric stratification. These thermodynamic shifts alter vertical refractivity gradients and can modulate atmospheric ducts, which are natural waveguides crucial for beyond-line-of-sight electromagnetic propagation. Using ERA5 reanalysis data from 1940 to 2025, we find a global-scale intensification of atmospheric ducts over oceans at mid- to low-latitude, with a robust increasing trend in atmospheric duct occurrence probability, strength and top height. Mechanistically, this intensification is intrinsically coupled with the sustained increase in static stability in the marine atmospheric boundary layer. Although interannual climate modes, such as the El Niño/Southern Oscillation, modulate these anomalies, the long-term warming trend dominates the long-term trend. Ultimately, continuous warming is shifting the marine atmospheric background state towards a highly stratified regime favouring more frequent and intense ducting, with implications for global maritime communication, radar and navigation systems.

title: Warming oceans hit the battlefield
abstract: Marine radar signal propagation is highly sensitive to fine-scale vertical changes in water vapour. Now research shows that long-term increases in sea surface temperatures are strengthening the frequency and intensity of the features that allow radar signals to travel further than expected.

title: Political affiliation impacts climate attention and choice beyond extreme weather exposure
abstract: Political polarization and increasing exposure to extreme weather can shape public engagement with climate change, yet the underlying psychological mechanisms remain unclear. In this Registered Report, we examine how political affiliation, extreme weather exposure and subjective attribution influence climate-relevant information search and decision-making in a US sample ( N = 1,451). We combined a process-tracing paradigm within an incentivized decision task involving real carbon emissions with objective data on extreme weather exposure. Democrats attended more to carbon emission information and made more pro-climate choices than Republicans, with no evidence of moderation by objective extreme weather exposure. The subjective attribution of extreme weather to climate change was associated with greater attention to carbon information, more pro-climate choices and moderated the effects of exposure on both outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of political affiliation in climate-relevant decision-making and suggest that extreme weather effects depend less on exposure itself than on how these experiences are interpreted.

title: Climate choices and attention are shaped more by politics than weather
abstract: Climate change will further increase the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events. Subjective experience and attribution of extreme weather events to climate change, rather than objective exposure alone, are associated with greater climate-relevant attention and choices. Political affiliation influences attention and behaviour irrespective of subjective attribution and objective exposure.

title: Astrid Schomaker on biodiversity in a triple COP year
abstract: This year, all three major Rio Conventions — on biodiversity, climate and desertification — convene their respective Conference of the Parties (COP). In advance of the biodiversity COP17, Astrid Schomaker, the executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, discusses the irrefutable need to integrate biodiversity conservation into broader environmental action to ensure local and global security and prosperity in a rapidly changing world.

title: Biodiversity and the Conferences of the Parties
abstract: In a year containing summits from the three United Nations environmental frameworks, we consider how cooperation across the Conferences of the Parties (COPs) can facilitate implementation and impact. Co-timed with the start of the biodiversity COP, we highlight the reciprocal relationship between climate change and biodiversity.

title: Rare diseases are an overlooked dimension in climate–health adaptation
abstract: A resilient society must prepare not only for common harms but also for uncommon vulnerabilities, such as rare disease where the consequences leave no room for failure. Ensuring that people with rare diseases have reliable access to essential care is crucial for fairness and safety in a changing climate.

title: Increased southward swings of the South Indian convergence zone under greenhouse warming
abstract: Extreme southward swings of the South Indian convergence zone can induce devastating floods over parts of southern Africa. How greenhouse warming affects such southward swings is not well understood. Here we show that, under a high-emissions scenario, the frequency of extreme southward swings doubles from one event per 22 years in the twentieth century to one per 10 years in the twenty-first century with an average increase in rainfall intensity of 20%. The increased frequency is related to faster warming of the African continent than of the Indian Ocean that intensifies northerly winds, and to a poleward migration of Southern Ocean westerlies that drives a pattern of faster subtropical Indian Ocean warming to the south and enhances Atlantic-to-Africa moisture transport, both of which favour a southward swing of the South Indian convergence zone. More frequent southward migration of the South Indian convergence zone might thus indicate increasing flooding risk in parts of southern Africa.

title: Targeting high-value uses to unlock the mitigation potential of clean hydrogen
abstract: Clean hydrogen is a versatile decarbonization option, but given its energy-intensive production, high costs and limited near-term supply, uses with the greatest environmental and economic benefits must be prioritized. Analysis of ten end-use sectors identifies high-value applications and suggests that uniform supply-side subsidies risk misallocating clean hydrogen and public funds, highlighting the need for sector-specific demand-side policies.

title: Climate warming boosts frequency and intensity of southern Africa’s rainfall extremes
abstract: Extreme southward swings of the South Indian convergence zone (a major source of rainfall across southern Africa) can trigger devastating floods. Climate-model projections indicate that these swings might occur twice as often in the twenty-first century as in the previous century and produce more intense rainfall, owing to an increased land–sea temperature contrast and poleward intensification of atmospheric circulation.

title: Reversal of Antarctic Intermediate Water trends triggered by sea ice decline
abstract: Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW), a key component of the global overturning circulation and a major regulator of pycnocline structure, forms in the polar Southern Ocean, where sea-ice processes shape its properties. Sustained sea-ice expansion over several decades up to 2015 enhanced summertime meltwater input, stratifying the upper polar ocean and freshening AAIW. However, since 2016, repeated record sea-ice losses have reversed these trends. Using Argo-derived ocean observations supplemented by satellite and re-analysis datasets, we reveal that the abrupt post-2015 shift in sea-ice conditions is on course to alter hemispheric-wide water-mass properties. We estimate a net decline in sea-ice meltwater input of nearly 36 mSv per decade, relative to a pre-2016 increase of 14 mSv per decade. This unprecedented sea-ice loss has triggered densification and salinification of AAIW, whose core has salinified at 4.8 × 10 −3 ± 1.7 × 10 −3 g kg −1 per decade. These changes signal that a hemispheric-scale reconfiguration of the pycnocline is underway.

title: Closing the climate–economics communication gap
abstract: As the IPCC is in its seventh assessment cycle, bridging the gap between physical climate science and economics has become more urgent. Estimating climate damages requires a rigorous translation of physical hazards into economic losses, highlighting the need for better communication between the disciplines.

title: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
abstract: Most coupled Earth system models do not include fully interactive ice sheets, introducing uncertainty in future projections of polar climate and global sea level. To this end, we conduct 100,000-year-long simulations for different CO 2 conditions using the community Earth system model coupled to the bihemispheric Penn State University ice sheet–ice shelf model. Whereas global warming exceeding 2 °C above pre-industrial conditions and related subsurface ocean warming lead to the millennial-scale disintegration of the West Antarctic ice sheet, the East Antarctic ice sheet shows a much greater resilience, even at 10 °C or more of warming. The simulations reveal that a moister and cloudier atmosphere over Antarctica, with southward-shifted westerlies, increases snow accumulation and reduces shortwave radiation. For Greenland, a 6 °C threshold above pre-industrial levels is identified. Capturing the balance of ocean- and atmosphere-driven ablation and accumulation processes in coupled climate–ice-sheet models will improve projections of long-term sea-level rise.

title: Southeast Asian voices on climate change
abstract: Responding to the increasing risks of climate change in Southeast Asia requires research and effective action that considers the unique challenges of the region. In this Viewpoint, researchers and practitioners from the region share their views on the progress made in understanding and responding to climate change.

title: Time to drop the no-policy business-as-usual baselines
abstract: Baseline construction shapes estimates of mitigation cost, ambition and progress, while no-policy counterfactuals could vary with choices about policy, technology and development. Rather than relying on one constructed baseline, assessments and related conclusions should be compared across plausible baselines.

title: Zero emissions commitment depends on warming level
abstract: When anthropogenic CO 2 emissions cease, global temperature does not stabilize immediately. The resulting global temperature change, the zero emissions commitment, is central to carbon budget assessments and understanding reversibility of global warming, yet its dependence on prior warming levels remains unclear. Here we show, using zero-emission simulations with the UK Earth System Model (UKESM1.2) across global warming levels of 1.5–5 K, that the zero emissions commitment stays near zero up to 2 K but becomes positive at higher warming levels, reaching 0.4–0.6 K after ~ 150 years. This dependence indicates that stabilizing or reversing warming becomes progressively more difficult as peak temperature rises. We identify the mechanism behind this behaviour: stronger warming from higher radiative disequilibrium and weakening carbon sinks, driven by saturated land carbon uptake and the reduced radiative impact of CO 2 drawdown at higher background CO 2 concentrations. Higher peak warming therefore commits the planet to additional warming, limiting temperature-overshoot reversibility.

title: Brazil’s data-driven plan for climate-resilient healthcare
abstract: By integrating climate risk into health planning, Brazil is redesigning healthcare to withstand floods, heatwaves and other climate shocks.
